## Cold Spring Weekend, Thu Feb 18 – Sat Feb 20

Round trip from South Slope. Follows the household's standard short-trip-with-Kibo shape: direct car travel, no multi-stop transfers, one longer outing with substantial downtime.

### Before booking
- Confirm this weekend is actually clear: check Devika's current 8-week hospital schedule and Alex's finalized Infra roster for Feb 18-20 — no hospital assignment/overnight coverage for Devika, no primary/secondary on-call interval for Alex. Don't commit to nonrefundable bookings until both are confirmed clear.
- Once confirmed, treat it as protected — decline optional work (on-call swaps, extra Infra tasks, review asks) that would land in this window.

- **Transport:** rental car (or own car), single direct drive each way — no interim stops. One ~10-15 min leashed water break at the drive's midpoint only.

- 0.875 cup breakfast, 0.875 cup dinner, 0.25 cup treats (portioned through the day), per the standing diet split.
- Any unused pouch on a travel day stays sealed and comes home — don't roll it into another day's ration.

### Kibo — other
- Bring current front-clip harness + leash, weight-appropriate coat/boots for February cold, towel for wet-gear wipe-down before re-entering the room.
- Confirm rabies certificate copy is packed (valid through Aug 2029).

pr.title: Emit blocked handoff observations from a retryable worker
pr.author: mira
pr.description: Moves quarterly handoff-observation writes off the readiness path. Queue delivery is at least once, and a job may be retried after a timeout.

files.patch:
def emit_observation(job):
    row = build_report_row(job.handoff, job.failure)
    row["observation_id"] = str(uuid4())
    row["subject_member_id"] = job.handoff.owner_member_id
    quarterly_handoff_observations.insert(row)
    job.ack()

def test_emits_blocked_handoff():
    emit_observation(job)
    assert observations.count() == 1
    assert observations.first().failure_details == job.failure.details

pr.review_notes: No retry or redelivery test is included.

input.body:
One failure-boundary gap in `emit_observation`: with at-least-once delivery, `observation_id` should be derived deterministically from stable job/handoff identity, not generated fresh per call.

Right now:
```
row["observation_id"] = str(uuid4())
quarterly_handoff_observations.insert(row)
job.ack()
```
If the job is redelivered after a timeout (ack lost, or a crash between insert and ack), this re-runs with a brand-new random id and inserts a second row for the same underlying handoff/failure — an unbounded duplicate quarterly observation rather than a safe retry.

Suggested fix: key `observation_id` off something intrinsic and stable across redeliveries — e.g. a hash/composite of `(job.handoff.id, job.failure.id)` or the queue's own message/job id if it's stable across redelivery — and make the write idempotent on that key (insert-if-not-exists / upsert) rather than a blind insert. That way retries land on the same row instead of producing duplicates.

Also worth adding the redelivery test the review notes call out: emit the same job twice and assert `observations.count() == 1`.

tests.request: Create a document containing a short incident-practice case study about the April 2023 metrics-router cutover canary, ending with two responder discussion questions.

input.title: Incident Practice Case Study: April 2023 Metrics-Router Cutover Canary
input.body:
## Background

In March–April 2023, the metrics pipeline was mid-migration in a fixed sequence: ingest-edge first (completed 2023-03-22), then metrics-router, then shard-keeper. Metrics-router's prod cutover followed a locked-in traffic schedule — 30% → 60% → 95% → 100% — with a 48-hour soak required at each step before advancing. By early April the rollout had progressed cleanly through 30% and 60%, and traffic had been pushed to roughly 80% as of 2023-04-06, holding without drops or latency anomalies.

## What happened

On 2023-04-07 at approximately 14:30 ET, an info-level canary alert fired on metrics-router during the cutover. The canary's auto-rollback mechanism triggered automatically, exactly as designed, pulling the affected cohort out of the traffic mix before it caused broader impact.

The responder investigated and identified the root cause: a regression in the OTel collector's batch window, not a defect in metrics-router's own application code. With the cause isolated, the responder redeployed and confirmed the fix was clean.

By 15:30 ET the same day, the manager (Hema) checked in directly after seeing the canary alert. The responder was able to tell her the rollback, redeploy, and clean confirmation were already done — nothing further needed from her side.

## Outcome

- No page was triggered — this stayed at info-level severity throughout.
- No user-facing impact.
- Total time to resolution: approximately 4 hours from alert to confirmed-clean redeploy.

document.title: Incident Practice Case Study: April 2023 Metrics-Router Cutover Canary
document.body:
## Background

In March–April 2023, the metrics pipeline was mid-migration in a fixed sequence: ingest-edge first (completed 2023-03-22), then metrics-router, then shard-keeper. Metrics-router's prod cutover followed a locked-in traffic schedule — 30% → 60% → 95% → 100% — with a 48-hour soak required at each step before advancing. By early April the rollout had progressed cleanly through 30% and 60%, and traffic had been pushed to roughly 80% as of 2023-04-06, holding without drops or latency anomalies.

## What happened

On 2023-04-07 at approximately 14:30 ET, an info-level canary alert fired on metrics-router during the cutover. The canary's auto-rollback mechanism triggered automatically, exactly as designed, pulling the affected cohort out of the traffic mix before it caused broader impact.

The responder investigated and identified the root cause: a regression in the OTel collector's batch window, not a defect in metrics-router's own application code. With the cause isolated, the responder redeployed and confirmed the fix was clean.

By 15:30 ET the same day, the manager (Hema) checked in directly after seeing the canary alert. The responder was able to tell her the rollback, redeploy, and clean confirmation were already done — nothing further needed from her side.

## Outcome

- No page was triggered — this stayed at info-level severity throughout.
- No user-facing impact.
- Total time to resolution: approximately 4 hours from alert to confirmed-clean redeploy.
- The responder posted a note to the team channel framing the event positively: the canary and auto-rollback tooling had caught a real regression before it could spread, which is the system working as intended rather than a failure.

tests.request: Create a shard-keeper runbook index entry for the April 18, 2023 outage, using its canonical incident ID as the title.

input.title: INC-2023-04-18-001
input.body:
Sev2 outage, 2023-04-18. Config push carrying a label-name change (shard-keeper label_map) shipped without rollup-service's owning side in the loop; rollup-service never picked up the change, so symptom-level alerts fired while the actual cause stayed silent underneath. Paged 21:42 ET; ~5h45m total duration; ingestion impaired for the window; no data loss. Rollback path was fragile at the time.

Root cause: config pushes propagated to shard-keeper only, not to all label-consuming downstream services.

Mitigations: permanent pre-push sync rule (no shard-keeper config push without syncing with the other owner/on-call); rollback path simplified to a single command (closed 2023-05-30); team-wide no-Friday-afternoon prod deploy policy adopted 2023-04-28.

- **What the review established:** across all three release cycles, the canonical versioned package plus generated downstream files produced no Figma-to-repository drift; the automated drift check caught one attempted Figma-only rename before it reached engineering; downstream files stayed reproducible from the versioned source.
- **What source must change:** only the canonical versioned token package. Downstream representations (including the Android JSON) are generated outputs, not editable sources — this line has held even under repeated proposals (a Figma-first exception, a 7-day platform-local override window, and a writeback of "newer-looking" generated values into canonical) and none were accepted.
- **How Android output is produced:** generated from the pinned canonical package by the platform generator — it is not maintained independently.
- **How drift is blocked:** an automated CI check compares generated output against the canonical package and blocks publish on generator failure or drift (fail-closed; generate to staging, promote only on success).
- **Trial status:** the pilot concluded and was formally adopted on 2026-09-13 — it's North Pier's ongoing workflow, not a continuing trial.

Given that, this PR edits `platform/android/generated/tokens.json` directly with no corresponding canonical-package change, which treats the generated Android file as an independent source of truth. That's the same shape as the platform-local-override pattern the workflow review already declined — the warning-token change should go into the canonical package instead, with Android regenerated from it.

input.title: Cardinality Guardrails parity fixture
input.body:
Check 3 (cross-service parity fixture, required since 2024-03-06 for covered shard-keeper/rollup-service label renames) validates the shared label contract with a bidirectional comparison, not a one-way containment check.

Accepted comparison (cardinality-guardrails#512, Roman's revision, 2026-04-03):
- Compares key presence in both directions: every expected key must be observed downstream AND every observed key must be expected upstream.
- Requires exact equality between each expected bounded-value set and the set actually observed from rollup-service (not just one-way containment).

This replaced an earlier one-directional version (flagged 2026-03-19) that only checked observed-subset-of-expected and would false-pass when a value silently failed to propagate downstream.

Pass case:
- Key-and-value sets match exactly between producer and rollup-service consumer (e.g. the retained shard_region -> storage_region fixture).

Fail cases:
- An expected value is missing downstream (fails).
- An unexpected value appears downstream that wasn't in the expected set (fails).

Status note: as of the 2026-04-03 revision, points 1-3 of the blocking review (bidirectional key check, bidirectional value-set equality, explicit failure on either missing-expected or unexpected-downstream cases) are satisfied. Point 4 (confirming the executed regression evidence also includes an existing passing case such as shard_region/storage_region) and affected-owner (shard-keeper/rollup-service) sign-off were still pending confirmation as of the last review. Production is unaffected either way.

tests.request: Inspect lantern#1688 and review its handling of stale, missing, and widely separated sources in combined customer explanations.

pr.title: lantern: assemble customer explanations from available service signals
pr.author: product-engineering
pr.description: Refactors the customer-preview explanation builder so independently usable deploy, ownership, and incident-load fragments can be composed without waiting for every adapter result.
change_summary: Lookup grouping remains keyed by tenant_id and published_service_id.
Each contributing adapter result must independently pass its existing freshness check and include provenance_source and source_timestamp.
When all three fragments pass those checks, buildExplanation emits one combined paragraph without comparing source timestamps across signal families.
When a family is stale or missing, its fragment is omitted; the remaining fragments are still composed into a partial explanation with a short availability clause.

fixtures.name: all_sources_fresh
fixtures.rendered_output: A recent deploy movement coincided with elevated incident load under the published Claims Ingest ownership.

fixtures.name: ownership_stale
fixtures.rendered_output: Deploy movement and elevated incident load describe the current service picture; ownership details are delayed.

input.body:
Provenance/source-time review (staying in my usual lane — this is a technical contract question, not an adoption or release call).

Stale and missing handling look correct: each fragment's freshness check runs independently, and a stale/missing family is omitted with an explicit availability clause rather than silently dropped or backfilled from another time field. That matches the standing source-registration acceptance rule (authoritative source_timestamp only, missing/malformed renders as explicit unknown, no substitution).

Gap: when all three fragments individually pass freshness, buildExplanation composes them into one paragraph without ever comparing source_timestamp across the signal families. The all_sources_fresh fixture shows this concretely — deploy at 2027-12-18T08:00:00Z, ownership at 2027-12-19T10:30:00Z, incident_load at 2027-12-19T12:15:00Z, roughly 28 hours apart end to end — rendered as "A recent deploy movement coincided with elevated incident load," which reads as a claim of temporal proximity/correlation the underlying timestamps don't actually support. Each fragment being individually fresh doesn't mean the fragments are close enough in time to combine into a coincidence-implying sentence; two widely separated but individually-fresh sources can currently produce the same "coincided" phrasing as two sources minutes apart.

This is the same class of ordering/combination question the acceptance rule was meant to cover, just at the cross-family composition step rather than within a single family: the rule requires using each record's authoritative source_timestamp for ordering, and I'd read that as extending to bounding how far apart source_timestamps can be before composing them into language that implies coincidence. Right now there's no such bound or disclosure when fragments are widely separated in time.

Requesting changes: either compare source_timestamp across families and add a separation/availability clause (similar to the stale/missing path) when the gap exceeds some bound, or soften the composed language so it doesn't imply temporal coincidence when the fragments weren't checked for proximity. Implementation approach and any threshold are Product Engineering's call — flagging the gap itself is what's in my lane.

output.body:
# Goal
First-cut controls for the Q4 Cardinality Guardrails work; keep it tied to the September mirror/replay legacy-aggregator wobble without turning validation movement into rollback criteria.

# First-cut matrix

## 1. Label limits
- Failure mode: unbounded or newly introduced label keys/values causing fanout.
- Candidate control: a narrow allowlist or budget per sensitive label family.
- Preflight: flag new high-cardinality labels before a metrics-router or shard-keeper push.

## 2. Alert-source semantics
- Failure mode: responders treating replay/mirror validation movement as live-path rollback evidence.
- Candidate control: dashboard and alert wording that marks live metrics-router traffic separately from replay or mirror validation samples.

## 3. Label-change preflight
- Failure mode: a config or parser change adding labels without checking cardinality behavior.
- Candidate control: a pre-push checklist with sample counts, source label, owner, and rollback/non-rollback semantics.

# Non-goals
- No customer-facing dashboard.
- No general telemetry rewrite.
- No legacy-aggregator retirement claim.
- No claim that the 2% replay sample creates immediate storage savings.
- No Q3 incident framing.

# Monday questions
- What cost examples can Cyrus bring by label family?
- Which preflight checks are service-owned by Alex versus data-platform advisory?
- What would make the first cut too broad?

## Bounded observability example — exception-review outcomes

The accepted production counter uses only these bounded labels:
- `service_pair_class`: `ingest_path`, `routing_path`, `ownership_path`, or `other`
- `exception_class`: `invariant`, `provenance`, `failure_mode`, `ownership`, or `escalation`
- `outcome`: `requested`, `accepted`, or `rejected`

Raw service names, owner email addresses, pull-request identifiers, and reviewer-supplied reasons remain in logs or audit records rather than metric labels. This example creates no centralized review owner: mapped owners retain implementation, operational, release, and rollback responsibility, while boundary review remains limited to the triggered cross-service exception.

output.title: INC-2023-10-30-001 metrics-router canary rollback — lightweight after-action
output.body:
# INC-2023-10-30-001 metrics-router canary rollback — lightweight after-action

## Summary
A metrics-router canary for `sha:b41c77a` was rolled back after live-path p99 and dropped writes moved on the canary slice. Replay and mirror validation panels were not the rollback trigger.

## Timeline
- 08:07 ET — Page fired for live metrics-router p99 on canary slice. Alex acknowledged the incident.
- 08:22 ET — Live-path p99 was around 118 ms, error rate was 0.18%, and dropped writes were 0.6% on the canary slice. Alex rolled back the most recent metrics-router deploy.
- 09:05 ET — p99 returned to about 46 ms, error rate returned to roughly 0.02%, and dropped writes returned to zero.

## What changed
The canary appears to have changed the `route_pattern` normalization path so one live handler emitted raw account/widget IDs instead of normalized route patterns. Replay validation still showed normalized route patterns, so replay evidence alone would not have caught the live hot-path value-shape change.

## Why rollback was appropriate
The signal was live-path metrics-router movement: p99 and dropped writes on the canary slice. Replay or mirror validation movement remains investigation evidence, not rollback criteria.

## Follow-ups
1. Keep the code fix small: restore normalized `route_pattern` values for the affected live handler before another canary.
2. Patch the Cardinality Guardrails checklist so live-path label value-shape changes require live canary evidence or a representative live-path fixture, not only replay validation.

## Non-goals
This note is not a broad incident postmortem, not a legacy-aggregator retirement discussion, and not a claim that Cardinality Guardrails is complete.

# Operating problem

Show how recurring cross-service and data-contract risks can be handled with explicit checks and escalation boundaries instead of relying on one person to review every case. The goal is reusable technical operating leverage, not a transfer of formal ownership or people management.

# Reusable mechanisms

- For covered Cardinality Guardrails changes, require an executable parity fixture and affected-owner signoff, alongside the relevant cardinality and alert-source checks, before production review.
- For Lantern, keep the ordinary admission lane with Iris while defining a clear exception boundary for escalated data-contract issues that need deeper schema, provenance, access, or downstream-semantics review.

These mechanisms improve how owners operate; they do not make Alex the owner of every covered review or every Lantern room. Iris retains ordinary Lantern admission decisions. Wes performs bounded first-pass checks within his practical scope, without Alex managing him or the formal owner map changing. Cross-service checks still require the affected owners and the appropriate service boundaries.

2. **Lantern ordinary lane versus exception boundary.** Iris can handle an ordinary admission decision. When a data-contract exception changes the meaning or safety of downstream data, it moves through the explicit exception boundary for focused technical review rather than silently being normalized in the ordinary lane.

# Cross-service gate exceptions — June 14 review

I define cross-service gates and escalation boundaries; I do not take over routine service operation or Iris's product interpretation.

## 1. Metrics-router generation-retirement thresholds

- **Invariant:** Pause additional configuration pushes if retired objects accumulate above four or cleanup pauses exceed 100 milliseconds. Preserve rollback for active-generation inconsistency, route divergence, or dropped series.
- **Observed evidence:** A single-file canary reached four retired generations and a 92-millisecond cleanup pause; the values approached but did not cross the thresholds, and the other consistency, parity, drop, reload, heap, and restart checks remained clean.
- **Current exception or uncertainty:** The event is near the pause boundaries; it does not establish that later pushes are safe without observation.
- **Mapped owner:** Metrics-router service ownership remains with the mapped service owner; Wes is the practical first-pass backup within the existing deploy rules.
- **Decision needed:** Whether the next configuration push may proceed one at a time.
- **Escalation condition:** Cross more than four retired objects or 100 milliseconds of cleanup pause, or observe active-generation inconsistency, route divergence, or dropped series.

## 2. Ingest-edge bounded decompression

- **Invariant:** Keep active decompression bounded at four per pod and two per tenant; preserve permit cleanup, body limits, accepted-point integrity, request-p99 rollback gates, and randomized one-, two-, and three-second Retry-After behavior.
- **Observed evidence:** Request p99 briefly rose 19 milliseconds above baseline; decode-wait p99 reached 188 milliseconds, waiting work reached eleven on the busiest pods, and one tenant represented 64% of queued requests. Active work stayed within the per-pod and per-tenant limits, permits returned to zero, oversized bodies were rejected before over-budget append, no accepted points were dropped, and no pod restarted.
- **Current exception or uncertainty:** The concentrated waiting queue raises a separate fairness and capacity question even though no rollback gate fired.
- **Mapped owner:** Ingest-edge routine operation remains with its mapped service owner; cross-service gate review remains with Alex.
- **Decision needed:** Leave the bounded-decompression release in production and define the owner-led fairness or capacity follow-up.
- **Escalation condition:** A production rollback gate fires, including a permit leak, active-work limit violation, dropped accepted points, or the applicable sustained request-p99 threshold.

- **Invariant:** Emit an external deploy event only when all required provenance validates; otherwise represent the result as explicit unknown with a machine-readable missing-provenance reason.
- **Observed evidence:** The corrected fixture rejects partial deploy objects, covers each missing required field with negative tests, performs authorization before lookup, and does not use internal room metadata or inferred ownership.

output.body:
# Oversized-batch design and staged enablement

## Selected permanent behavior
- Participating SDKs reject batches above 8,000 points before transmission.
- The local error tells callers to split the batch before retrying.
- Ingest-edge retains a deterministic backstop for older or nonconforming clients.
- The backstop returns HTTP 413, accepts zero points, reports rejected points equal to the submitted count, and uses the machine-readable `oversized_batch` reason.
- Clients must not retry an unchanged oversized request.

## Evidence behind the decision
- Current SDK clients rejected oversized attempts locally without network transmission.
- Split compliant requests reconciled accepted-point accounting.
- The older client received the deterministic ingest-edge response, made no unchanged retry, and succeeded after splitting.
- The corrected SDK error text names the 8,000-point maximum and the split-before-retry action.

## Enablement window
Stage enablement through January 28, with participating SDK prevention first and ingest-edge retained as the server-side backstop.

## Verification and stop checks
- No unchanged retry after local rejection or HTTP 413.
- Accepted plus rejected points reconcile to submitted points.
- Split requests do not duplicate or lose points.
- Compliant traffic remains at baseline error and latency levels.

The design is selected; this document does not claim staged enablement is complete.

## Evidence

output.title: Lantern published service alias rule — May 14 decision
output.body:
# Deployed status — May 28, 2026

Product Engineering deployed Lantern PR 1089's tenant-scoped published-service alias resolution for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce on May 28, 2026.

# Resolution rule

Lantern may resolve a historical service identifier only when the tenant-scoped owner map publishes an alias record containing the old identifier, the canonical published service identifier, and an effective interval covering the source event's timestamp. Both the effective interval's start timestamp and end timestamp are inclusive, so a source event timestamp equal to either endpoint is covered.

If no such record exists, the source event timestamp is earlier than the inclusive start timestamp, or the source event timestamp is later than the inclusive end timestamp, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown. The UI does not infer a rename from similar names or customer context.

# Harbor Health result

The original Harbor Health `claims-edge` event now resolves to published `claims-ingest` ownership because its source timestamp is covered by the owner map's published alias interval.

# Regression evidence

Across 28 executed fixtures:
- All 12 valid in-interval aliases joined to their canonical published service identifiers.
- Eight out-of-interval aliases remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.
- Eight identifiers with no published alias record remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.

# Affected safety rerun

Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

# Approved customer-facing wording

Authorized join: `Published service identity resolved from an owner-map alias effective at this source event timestamp.`

No qualifying alias: `Ownership unknown: no published owner-map alias covers this source event timestamp.`

# Unchanged boundary

The deployment applies only to Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. It adds no heuristic identity inference and does not expand the customer data contract.

## July 3, 2026 — deployed overlap correction

Lantern now evaluates every tenant-scoped owner-map alias whose inclusive effective interval covers the source event timestamp. If all qualifying records identify the same canonical published service, Lantern resolves that identity once. If qualifying records identify two or more distinct canonical services, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown regardless of storage order. Both effective-interval endpoints remain inclusive.

Executed regressions show the overlapping Harbor Health `claims-ingest` and `claims-router` records failing closed in both row orders, both inclusive endpoints working, and a single valid match resolving normally. Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

The correction is live for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. Their two-account read-only scope and customer data contract remain unchanged.

# Authority-record time semantics — March 18 brown-bag

## Authoritative source time
`source_timestamp` represents the original authoritative time of the underlying authority record. Later observation, serialization, processing, retry, and navigation times may be recorded as separate metadata, but they must not replace or refresh `source_timestamp`.

If a required source timestamp is missing or malformed, downstream navigation fails closed to explicit unknown.

When one card carries multiple authority references, each reference retains its own `source_timestamp`. An envelope time, render time, processing time, or newest retry time must not be substituted for any reference's authoritative source time.

output.body:
# Q4 incident practice — November 18 scoring sheet

## Scope
A bounded tabletop scoring sheet, not a production runbook. Score observable responder behavior for an accepted metrics-router action across cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, and publication.

## Core criteria
1. Durable attempt identity
- Pass: Responders identify the durable acceptance boundary and preserve one attempt identity after acceptance.
- Fail: They create, assume, or accept multiple identities for the same accepted attempt.

2. Terminal accounting
- Pass: Every accepted attempt reaches exactly one terminal result.
- Fail: An accepted attempt has no terminal result or exposes conflicting terminal results.

3. Failure classification
- Pass: Responders distinguish cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, and publication using the acceptance boundary.
- Fail: They collapse those cases or treat a pre-acceptance event as evidence about accepted work.

## Wes — responder path
Responders must first determine whether durable acceptance occurred before interpreting cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, or publication. After acceptance, they must preserve one durable attempt identity and exactly one terminal result.

## Nadia — postmortem criteria
The postmortem must name the absent system guarantee or control. It must not treat the triggering operator action as the root cause, and it must retain the mapped implementation and rollback owner.

## Final ownership-boundary condition
- Pass: Mapped owners retain implementation and rollback decisions, while the triggered reviewer remains confined to the named failure-mode boundary.
- Fail: The triggered review is treated as implementation, release, or rollback approval.

## Additional operating checks — November 8

### 45-minute secondary boundary
- Pass: When the cause remains unisolated, responders engage the secondary before the 45-minute boundary and make the incident clock visible.
- Fail: Responders wait until or after 45 minutes, or continue without engaging the secondary while the cause remains unisolated.

### Friday staging preparation versus production change
- Pass: Responders identify staging preparation that makes no production state change as staging work and separately identify a Friday-afternoon production deploy as prohibited.
- Fail: Responders classify staging-only preparation as a production deploy, or permit a Friday-afternoon production state change because it was described as preparation.

These checks supplement the accepted cancellation, caller-disconnect, durable-attempt, terminal-result, mapped-owner, and postmortem criteria. This remains a tabletop scoring sheet rather than a production runbook.

## November 18 execution order

- 5 minutes: role and ownership framing.
- 35 minutes: cancellation and caller-disconnect scenario.
- 10 minutes: one targeted rerun if a scoring boundary is missed.
- 10 minutes: debrief and owner follow-up.

Wes teaches the responder path. Nadia owns the postmortem section. Alex maintains only the bounded failure case. This is the exact one-hour tabletop sequence and does not turn the scoring sheet into a production runbook.

## Observed results — November 18

The tabletop is complete. Responders correctly separated durable acceptance from cancellation, caller disconnect, and process recovery; preserved one attempt identity and one terminal result in the exercise; identified Wes as the mapped metrics-router implementation, release, and rollback owner; and distinguished Friday staging preparation from a production change.

The first run engaged the secondary at minute 47 while the cause remained unisolated, missing the required before-45-minute boundary. The targeted rerun engaged the secondary at minute 42 and passed that boundary. Nadia’s debrief named the missing system control rather than the triggering operator action as root cause.

These results are training evidence only. The tabletop did not execute the product implementation and does not close any product defect or replace required executable product evidence.

## Training Appendix: INC-2023-04-18-001 (shard-keeper)

**The misleading early investigation branch**
When paged at 21:42, initial debugging went down a network-layer red herring before finding the real cause. Symptom-level alerts (ingestion impairment) fired loudly while the actual cause stayed silent — the shard-keeper label-name change had never propagated to rollup-service, a downstream consumer, so cause-level alerting never lit up. That silence made the network layer look like the natural first suspect, and time was lost chasing it before the label-name diff was found.

*Lesson:* when symptom alerts and cause alerts don't line up, don't fully trust the first plausible signal during triage — treat an early "root cause" as provisional until checked against what's actually observable.

**Confirmed data impact**
- No data loss.
- Ingestion impaired for ~5h45m total.
- Rollback was fragile — looked reversible on paper, wasn't once state had partially moved. On-call deliberately avoided widening scope or moving faster to compensate, to avoid making it worse.

**Root cause**
Shard-keeper's label-name change (signed off by Nadia) shipped in a config push without rollup-service — the downstream consumer of that label output — being represented in the sign-off. The change never propagated downstream, so shard-keeper and rollup-service disagreed on labels, producing symptom alerts with no corresponding cause signal.

**Resulting process changes**
1. No Friday-afternoon prod deploys — became Sphere-wide policy.
2. Page the secondary on-call within 45 minutes if the primary is still actively working an incident.
3. Runbook ownership audit, with cross-review from any team owning a touched downstream service.
4. Permanent rule: no shard-keeper config push without a pre-push sync with the other owner/on-call.

pr.title: docs: add owner-led canary response playbook
pr.author: wes
pr.body: This adds `docs/operations/owner-led-canary-response.md` as a standalone response playbook for owner-led metrics-router configuration windows. During those windows, operators are directed to follow the new file's stop and recovery flow instead of the general canary-response runbook. The existing `rb_metrics_router_canary` entry is intentionally left unchanged, with the two documents to be maintained side by side.

files.summary: Standalone owner-led-window response procedure with its own stop and recovery flow.

input.body:
Reviewed. Before this merges I'd like the split-document approach reconsidered, or at minimum reconciled explicitly.

**Core concern: two documents governing the same procedure will drift.** `rb_metrics_router_canary` already covers owner-led configuration windows end to end (opening decision, in-window thresholds, stop conditions, recovery sequencing, rollback triggers). That content isn't static prose — it's been built up incrementally over multiple real incidents (retired-generation/cleanup-pause thresholds, the host-maintenance rejoin gate, the clock-skew isolation split, stale-label parity-preflight stops), and it already went through one drift incident (2024-10-03) where the written reference fell out of sync with what was actually being practiced and had to be corrected and re-validated against production records before Hema would accept it for standing use. Standing up a second, independently-maintained playbook for the same window type reintroduces that same drift risk on day one, and now with two documents to keep in sync instead of one.

**Specific gaps I can't confirm from the PR description alone** — the summary says the new file has "its own stop and recovery flow" but doesn't say whether it inherits:
- The current numeric thresholds (retired generations ≤4/pod, cleanup pause ≤100ms) and the "OR, not AND" pause/rollback logic
- The full-health-set return-to-baseline requirement after every push
- The recovery sequencing rule specifically: a post-stop fresh decision authorizes exactly one fully observed push — it does not reopen a multi-push window (this exact point required a live correction during the Aug 2025 Wes/Alex walkthrough, so it's evidently easy to get wrong even for people close to the process)
- The always-active rollback triggers (consistency, parity, dropped series, reload, restart) that apply regardless of window state
- The 2025-04-15 host-maintenance rejoin gate and the 2025-06-20 clock-skew/host-isolation split — both closed real gaps in the existing runbook and would be silent regressions if the new doc doesn't carry them forward

**Ask:** either (a) fold this content into `rb_metrics_router_canary` as an owner-led-window section rather than a separate file, so there's one authoritative document, or (b) if a separate file is genuinely warranted, have it explicitly reference/inherit the accepted thresholds and rollback-trigger set from `rb_metrics_router_canary` rather than restating them, and state precisely which situations route to which document. "Two documents maintained side by side" without that reconciliation is the part I'd block on — not the idea of an owner-led-window playbook itself.

Not an ownership question — doesn't change the owner map (Alex primary, Wes backup) either way.

entries.title: shard-keeper: rollback procedure (post-Apr-18 hardened path)
entries.body:
1. Remove the affected replica from follower reads.
2. Verify that the lease holder and epoch remain stable, with no acquisition or relinquishment events, stale-owner messages, overlapping leadership, or write errors.
3. Confirm that the replica is making forward catch-up progress.
4. Re-enter the follower read pool only after disk latency is back at baseline and lag is below one second for fifteen continuous minutes.
5. Restart only if the replica stops progressing after the lease-safety checks. Do not use an automatic timer response as the restart condition.

entries.title: shard-keeper: verify lease convergence after failover
entries.body:
Process readiness alone is not the exit condition. In the staging failover drill, all replacement replicas reported ready after 18 seconds, but lease ownership did not converge until 96 seconds. Before declaring the failover complete, verify all of the following: 1. Every partition has exactly one owner. 2. Lease epochs remain monotonic. 3. No stale-owner messages appear for two full lease-renewal intervals. If any of those checks fail, keep the failover open and page the shard-keeper owner. Renewal-warning versus lease transfer: `renewal deadline exceeded` alone does not prove a lease transfer. Check for a changed lease epoch, explicit acquisition or relinquishment, overlapping leadership, and post-event replication convergence. If the holder and epoch remain unchanged, no overlap occurs, and lag returns to baseline, treat the event as a delayed renewal rather than a failover; do not automatically restart.

## Production lease-loss serving-gate invariant

On lease-loss notification, close the old holder's serving gate before it can return another routing response. The periodic poll is only a backup detector, not the serving-safety mechanism. Production verification must include:
- gate closure before any later routing response
- exactly one serving holder throughout the transfer
- lease-loss notification to gate-close latency
- stale routing responses
- replacement acquisition time
- request p99
- errors
- restarts

A slow handoff or convergence warning is an availability signal to investigate separately. By itself, it is not evidence that the old holder served after lease loss or that the serving-safety invariant failed. The owner map and mapped deployment responsibility remain unchanged.

tests.answer:
Empty working directory, so here's the case study as text — let me know if you'd like it saved as a file or doc instead.

---

## Cardinality Guardrails — Onboarding Case Study #1: First Prevention

**Program:** Cardinality Guardrails (metrics-router / shard-keeper / rollup-service label-change checklist)
**Date of incident:** Nov 14, 2023
**Check involved:** Check 1 — label-cardinality preflight

### What was proposed
A new rollup-service validation metric:

```
rollup_validation_sample_total{
  validation_result="match|mismatch",
  replay_source_id="$source_id"
}
```

### What the checklist caught
Check 1 requires showing whether a label's value set is bounded, expected-high-cardinality-with-an-owner, or effectively unbounded. A sample pulled by Cyrus showed `replay_source_id` grows without bound across replay sources, jobs, chunks, and backfills — there's no fixed catalog of values. The proposal failed check 1 before it shipped.

### Resolution
- Kept the raw `replay_source_id` in **logs** for debugging/drill-down.
- Added a bounded `source_class` label on the **metric** for rollup-service validation dashboards.
- Same visibility for on-call, no unbounded label on the hot metric.

### Why it matters for onboarding
This is the first case where the checklist stopped a bad label shape *before* it reached production, rather than just clarifying wording after the fact. It also became the template for every later raw-identifier finding — the same bounded-classification-label / raw-value-in-logs split was reapplied to `template_revision_sha` (Dec 1, 2023), `origin_build_sha` (Jan 19, 2024), and `refusal_reason` (Mar 2025).

### The reusable question set (generalized Nov 23, 2023)
When a raw identifier shows up as a proposed label, ask:
1. Is the value set bounded and named, or can it grow with requests/jobs/tenants/chunks/backfills/arbitrary records?
2. Does the dashboard/alert actually need it as a metric dimension, or is it only needed for debugging?
3. If unbounded, keep it in logs/trace context, not the metric label set.
4. If grouping is genuinely needed, use a bounded classification label (e.g. `source_class`) instead of the raw value.

**Takeaway for new reviewers:** this case is the canonical example of what "check 1 catches" looks like in practice — cite it, don't re-derive the reasoning, when a raw ID/SHA/error string shows up as a proposed label.

**Cardinality Guardrails — Original First Release: Historical Scope Note**

**Effort origin:** Opened 2023-10-10 at Hema's request, turning the September mirror/replay cardinality wobble into a named controls effort. Alex owns the effort end-to-end (design, first-cut implementation, router-level enforcement); Cyrus/data platform role is advisory only (cost-model input), explicitly not enforcement ownership.

**Original three-check scope, locked 2023-10-24** (with Cyrus, Nadia, Roman):
1. **Label-cardinality preflight** — for metrics-router and shard-keeper label changes.

tests.answer:
## Lantern PR 1602 — "stabilize mixed-source chronology" (Harbor Health, Mosaic Commerce)

**Ordering control:** The visible order is controlled by `processed_at`, not `source_timestamp`:
```
records.sort((a, b) => b.processed_at.localeCompare(a.processed_at))
```
`source_timestamp` is only consumed by `parseSourceTimestamp` for the presence/validity check, not for ordering.

This directly contradicts the standing acceptance rule from [[project_source_time_ordering_acceptance_rule]], reconfirmed on PR 1547: authoritative `source_timestamp` must control ordering, and `processed_at` must **never** be used — not even as a tiebreaker. PR 1602 uses it as the *primary* sort key.

**Timestamps current policy treats as audit-only:** `observed_at`, `serialized_at`, `processed_at`, `retry_at` — all four are carried on the record but must not affect order. `processed_at` being the actual sort key is the violation, not an acceptable audit-only use.

**Missing/malformed required source_timestamp:** Per the `malformed_required_source_timestamp` fixture, the whole result collapses to `{ chronology: [] }` — an empty list. The accepted rule requires rendering an **explicit unknown**, not silent suppression. An empty chronology is indistinguishable from "no records exist," which loses the fault signal for Harbor Health/Mosaic Commerce rather than surfacing it.

**Claims this chronology may currently make:** none regarding source-time order. It can only be described as *processing-order* chronology. The `delayed_retry` fixture's correct-looking result (`incident_load` before `deploy_event`) is coincidental to that fixture's numbers, not a guarantee of the algorithm — nothing in the sort ties the outcome to `source_timestamp`. It also cannot claim that a missing/malformed source timestamp is flagged to the customer; it can only claim the chronology is dropped entirely in that case.

This is a source-time/contract question, so it's in my review lane per [[feedback_review_question_lane_classification]] — flagging it as a rule violation for Mira/Product Engineering to fix, not a merge or release call. Want me to file this via `review_pr` as `request_changes`?

input.title: Secondary-page deadline
input.body:
Rule: the secondary must be engaged (paged/pulled in) before the 45-minute mark when an issue isn't resolving. This threshold comes from the 2023-04-28 postmortem.

Wes's June 21, 2023 example: on his first solo shard-keeper shift, Wes hit a minor metrics-router cardinality blip and pulled in the secondary at the 40-minute mark once he was unsure — inside the 45-minute deadline. This was scored as correct use of the rule, not a readiness gap. Later the same night, a second, smaller page cleared on its own by the 25-minute mark, so he let it ride without escalating — also correct, since escalation is only required if the issue is still unresolved as the 45-minute boundary approaches.

How to apply: when evaluating a responder's handling of an incident, check whether the secondary was engaged before 45 minutes elapsed on any issue that was still open. Escalating earlier (as in the 40-minute case) is fine; not escalating at all is fine only if the issue resolved on its own before the boundary. Escalating late, or not at all when the issue is still open past 45 minutes, is the failure mode this deadline is meant to catch.

tests.request: Create a concise implementation checklist for future changes to Lantern's locked v0 data and UI boundary.
tests.answer:
Based on Lantern's accumulated data-contract and rehearsal history, here's a concise checklist for any future change touching the locked v0 data/UI boundary:

**1. Authorization-before-lookup**
Every source adapter call must go through the shared authorization wrapper. Denied requests must make **zero adapter invocations** — verify via call-count/mock assertions, not by inspecting response content. (Content-clean and order-clean are separate properties; a 2024-07-12 run passed one and failed the other.)

**2. Source-timestamp authority**
Ordering/freshness must use each record's own authoritative `source_timestamp`. Never substitute or refresh with fetch/processing/render/retry/generation time. Missing or malformed required timestamp → explicit `unknown`, not a fallback field.

**3. Sentinel vocabulary, no coercion**
Keep `unknown` / `suppressed` / `unavailable` / `not_authorized` distinct at the API layer even if UI renders some identically. Never coerce a missing source to a populated value (e.g. `0/0`, `basic`) and never add a hybrid populated+flag shape (`stale: true` was explicitly rejected). A record aged past its pipeline's own freshness limit collapses to the same `unknown` shape as no-record-at-all.

**4. Tenant isolation**
Any cache/lookup key must include tenant identity. Confirm with an actual witnessed cross-tenant rehearsal (two synthetic tenants, same service identifier) — a design/fixture report alone doesn't establish this.

**5. Zero-tolerance content scan**
Negative fixtures must reject raw incident text, internal room metadata, employee identifiers, internal-only IDs, and comparison/breakdown fields. Any single leak fails the whole run — not a partial fail.

**6. 24-hour correlation rule (Lantern#84, locked)**
Compute timestamp spread from elapsed source instants, never truncated calendar dates (past bug class). Signals >24h apart render as separate cards with a no-causal-language flag. This rule is formally reviewed and locked — don't loosen it without a new formal review.

**7. Authority-record coherence**
`authority_type`, `authority_record_id`, and `source_timestamp` must all resolve to the *same* named authority — never mix an enforcement-point ID (e.g. metrics-router) with the authority's own record ID.

**8. Reference-only, no second authority**
No copying authority payload values into Lantern, no mutation endpoints. Lantern stays a consumer/navigator, never a second authority or write path.

**9. Design/sheet completion ≠ execution**
A completed rehearsal plan or passing individual fixtures are not equivalent to a witnessed combined run. Report execution results distinctly, cumulative (not per-slice) against all acceptance conditions.

**10. Scope discipline in write-ups**
A clean technical/security pass is evidence only — never describe it as a customer-access, rollout, or scope-expansion decision.

tests.request: Create a metrics-router runbook entry listing every stop condition for the bounded queue and backpressure rollout.

input.title: Bounded Queue & Backpressure Rollout — Stop Conditions
input.body:
Scope: global queue cap 2,048 batches; per-tenant cap 64 pending batches; overflow routes into the existing retryable backpressure path before acceptance (queue-full requests are rejected with 429 + Retry-After — already-admitted work is never evicted).

Stop conditions (any one of the following halts the active rollout stage):
1. queue_wait_p99_ms{source_class="live_production"} > 400ms, sustained for 5 continuous minutes.
2. retryable_queue_full_ratio{source_class="live_production"} > 0.5%, sustained for 5 continuous minutes.
3. Any accepted batch (points already admitted) is lost.
4. Any of the following checks departs from baseline: consistency, parity, dropped-series, route, shard-keeper-lease, rollup-service, or the full-health check set.

Notes:
- Alerting distinguishes cause vs symptom: queue_wait_p99 breach = saturation/cause signal; retryable_queue_full_ratio breach = refusal/symptom signal. Only source_class=live_production may page; staged_validation/replay sources do not.
- "5 minutes" means sustained breach (five continuous minutes above threshold), not a single data point.
- No per-tenant cap breach alone is a stop condition unless it drives one of the above thresholds.
- Stage sequencing: 10% → verify opening evidence + full-health baseline → 50% → verify again → 100%, with no production push on Fridays (monitoring only).
- Owners: Wes — implementation, load-test evidence, and capacity-related production-window opening decisions; Alex — cross-service invariants and failure-mode boundary (opens the window if Wes unavailable); Cyrus/Roman — rollup-service capacity and parity evidence; Nadia — queue/refusal alert semantics and ownership.

pr.description: The catalog-sync card currently displays `Unknown owner`. This patch adds a static `Product Engineering` owner value to the card configuration so the UI can display an owner immediately.

input.body:
Flagging a provenance concern before this merges.

This patch replaces the "Unknown owner" state with a static hard-coded value ("Product Engineering") in the card config. tests.request: Create a facilitator sheet for Hema's quarterly Infra onboarding module using its three adopted incident-practice scenarios and scoring rules.

input.title: Quarterly Infra Onboarding Module — Facilitator Sheet
input.body:
**Purpose:** Facilitator reference for Hema's standing quarterly infra-rotation onboarding module. Training/tabletop use only — not a production runbook, on-call procedure, or ownership change.

**Owner split (unchanged since adoption):**
- Wes — teaches the responder-path scenarios; also syncs responder-path content whenever the underlying rotation runbook changes a branch
- Nadia — reviews the postmortem section
- Alex — maintains the cross-service failure-case section only (not responder-path or postmortem content, not implementation/release/rollback sign-off)

---

## Three adopted scenarios

1. **Replacement readiness budget.** A replacement instance misses its fixed readiness budget without becoming routable.
   - Pass: responders keep the over-budget replacement unroutable and do not treat a restart as acceptance evidence.
   - Fail: responders route to the replacement anyway, or count a restart as proof of readiness.

2. **Cancellation race / terminal result.** A cancellation race must preserve exactly one terminal result and one matching accounting contribution.
   - Pass: responders resolve to a single terminal winner with one matching accounting contribution.
   - Fail: responders count both cancellation and completion as terminal (double-counts the outcome).

3. **Replay vs. live rollback evidence.** Replay samples must not be presented as live rollback criteria.
   - Pass: responders treat missing source classification as ineligible for live rollback evidence.
   - Fail: responders accept replay/mirrored samples as sufficient grounds for a live rollback decision.

---

## Scoring rules (runbook statements — test all three every cycle)

1. **Incident clock / secondary engagement.** Pass criterion is *primary engages the secondary before the 45-minute boundary* when isolation has failed — not secondary acknowledgment time. Acknowledgment latency is recorded separately and must not alter the escalation-timing result. (Corrected 2025-04-01 after a worksheet scoring error conflated the two.)

2. **Change classification (Friday prep vs. Friday deploy).** Pass: responder identifies Friday-afternoon staging prep with no production-state change as permitted, and separately identifies any Friday-afternoon production-state change as a prohibited deploy — held for Monday regardless of how ready staging looks. Fail: treating staging-only prep as itself a prohibited deploy, or waving through a production change on "it's just finishing what staging already validated."

3. **Missing system control, not operator blame.** The postmortem must name the missing system guardrail as root cause, not the triggering operator action.

**Note:** These three statements are the scoring backbone and must be preserved cycle to cycle — don't let the module drift into generic incident-response trivia.

---

## Standing caveats for the facilitator

- All three scenarios and scoring rules are training/tabletop only; passing or failing a cycle does not close a product defect, authorize a production change, or alter any owner's mapped scope.
- Section ownership stays separate — do not merge Wes's, Nadia's, and Alex's contributions into a single shared section.

output.title: Cardinality Guardrails — first failure-mode matrix
output.body:
# Goal
First-cut controls for the Q4 Cardinality Guardrails work; keep it tied to the September mirror/replay legacy-aggregator wobble without turning validation movement into rollback criteria.

# First-cut matrix

## 1. Label limits
- Failure mode: unbounded or newly introduced label keys/values causing fanout.
- Candidate control: a narrow allowlist or budget per sensitive label family.
- Preflight: flag new high-cardinality labels before a metrics-router or shard-keeper push.

## 2. Alert-source semantics
- Failure mode: responders treating replay/mirror validation movement as live-path rollback evidence.
- Candidate control: dashboard and alert wording that marks live metrics-router traffic separately from replay or mirror validation samples.

## 3. Label-change preflight
- Failure mode: a config or parser change adding labels without checking cardinality behavior.
- Candidate control: a pre-push checklist with sample counts, source label, owner, and rollback/non-rollback semantics.

# Non-goals
- No customer-facing dashboard.

# INC-2023-10-30-001 metrics-router canary rollback — lightweight after-action

## Summary
A metrics-router canary for `sha:b41c77a` was rolled back after live-path p99 and dropped writes moved on the canary slice. Replay and mirror validation panels were not the rollback trigger.

## Timeline
- 08:07 ET — Page fired for live metrics-router p99 on canary slice. Alex acknowledged the incident.
- 08:22 ET — Live-path p99 was around 118 ms, error rate was 0.18%, and dropped writes were 0.6% on the canary slice. Alex rolled back the most recent metrics-router deploy.
- 09:05 ET — p99 returned to about 46 ms, error rate returned to roughly 0.02%, and dropped writes returned to zero.

## What changed
The canary appears to have changed the `route_pattern` normalization path so one live handler emitted raw account/widget IDs instead of normalized route patterns. Replay validation still showed normalized route patterns, so replay evidence alone would not have caught the live hot-path value-shape change.

## Why rollback was appropriate
The signal was live-path metrics-router movement: p99 and dropped writes on the canary slice. Replay or mirror validation movement remains investigation evidence, not rollback criteria.

## Follow-ups
1. Keep the code fix small: restore normalized `route_pattern` values for the affected live handler before another canary.
2. Patch the Cardinality Guardrails checklist so live-path label value-shape changes require live canary evidence or a representative live-path fixture, not only replay validation.

## Non-goals
This note is not a broad incident postmortem, not a legacy-aggregator retirement discussion, and not a claim that Cardinality Guardrails is complete.

# Cross-service gate exceptions — June 14 review

I define cross-service gates and escalation boundaries; I do not take over routine service operation or Iris's product interpretation.

## 1. Metrics-router generation-retirement thresholds

- **Invariant:** Pause additional configuration pushes if retired objects accumulate above four or cleanup pauses exceed 100 milliseconds. Preserve rollback for active-generation inconsistency, route divergence, or dropped series.
- **Observed evidence:** A single-file canary reached four retired generations and a 92-millisecond cleanup pause; the values approached but did not cross the thresholds, and the other consistency, parity, drop, reload, heap, and restart checks remained clean.
- **Current exception or uncertainty:** The event is near the pause boundaries; it does not establish that later pushes are safe without observation.
- **Mapped owner:** Metrics-router service ownership remains with the mapped service owner; Wes is the practical first-pass backup within the existing deploy rules.
- **Decision needed:** Whether the next configuration push may proceed one at a time.
- **Escalation condition:** Cross more than four retired objects or 100 milliseconds of cleanup pause, or observe active-generation inconsistency, route divergence, or dropped series.

## 2. Ingest-edge bounded decompression

- **Invariant:** Keep active decompression bounded at four per pod and two per tenant; preserve permit cleanup, body limits, accepted-point integrity, request-p99 rollback gates, and randomized one-, two-, and three-second Retry-After behavior.
- **Observed evidence:** Request p99 briefly rose 19 milliseconds above baseline; decode-wait p99 reached 188 milliseconds, waiting work reached eleven on the busiest pods, and one tenant represented 64% of queued requests. Active work stayed within the per-pod and per-tenant limits, permits returned to zero, oversized bodies were rejected before over-budget append, no accepted points were dropped, and no pod restarted.
- **Current exception or uncertainty:** The concentrated waiting queue raises a separate fairness and capacity question even though no rollback gate fired.
- **Mapped owner:** Ingest-edge routine operation remains with its mapped service owner; cross-service gate review remains with Alex.
- **Decision needed:** Leave the bounded-decompression release in production and define the owner-led fairness or capacity follow-up.
- **Escalation condition:** A production rollback gate fires, including a permit leak, active-work limit violation, dropped accepted points, or the applicable sustained request-p99 threshold.

## 3. Lantern deploy provenance

- **Invariant:** Emit an external deploy event only when all required provenance validates; otherwise represent the result as explicit unknown with a machine-readable missing-provenance reason.
- **Observed evidence:** The corrected fixture rejects partial deploy objects, covers each missing required field with negative tests, performs authorization before lookup, and does not use internal room metadata or inferred ownership.
- **Current exception or uncertainty:** Guarded internal validation is active, but customer access remains closed; no external preview access is granted by this correction.
- **Mapped owner:** Alex defines the external data and failure-mode requirements; Iris leads product interpretation.
- **Decision needed:** Approve the fail-closed correction and focused tests without broadening the external contract.
- **Escalation condition:** Any implementation emits partial provenance, consults internal-only metadata, or treats guarded internal validation as customer access.

## 4. Rollup correction backlog

- **Invariant:** Correction processing must preserve assignment epochs, complete assignment snapshots, minimum-watermark evaluation, matching checkpoints and compaction IDs, and duplicate-free publication.
- **Observed evidence:** The correction-backlog evidence is still under review.
- **Current exception or uncertainty:** The backlog increase must be distinguished between bounded backfill and a stuck correction loop, checkpoint mismatch, duplicate processing, or publication risk.
- **Mapped owner:** Cyrus's data-platform team retains rollup-service implementation and operational ownership.

output.title: Oversized-batch design and staged enablement — through January 28
output.body:
# Oversized-batch design and staged enablement

## Selected permanent behavior
- Participating SDKs reject batches above 8,000 points before transmission.
- The local error tells callers to split the batch before retrying.
- Ingest-edge retains a deterministic backstop for older or nonconforming clients.
- The backstop returns HTTP 413, accepts zero points, reports rejected points equal to the submitted count, and uses the machine-readable `oversized_batch` reason.
- Clients must not retry an unchanged oversized request.

## Evidence behind the decision
- Current SDK clients rejected oversized attempts locally without network transmission.
- Split compliant requests reconciled accepted-point accounting.
- The older client received the deterministic ingest-edge response, made no unchanged retry, and succeeded after splitting.
- The corrected SDK error text names the 8,000-point maximum and the split-before-retry action.

## Enablement window
Stage enablement through January 28, with participating SDK prevention first and ingest-edge retained as the server-side backstop.

## Verification and stop checks
- No unchanged retry after local rejection or HTTP 413.
- Accepted plus rejected points reconcile to submitted points.
- Split requests do not duplicate or lose points.
- Compliant traffic remains at baseline error and latency levels.

The design is selected; this document does not claim staged enablement is complete.

## Role boundary

1. the affected component;

Nadia owns this front-door check. If any one of the four items is absent, including when the condition is only placeholder text such as `needs review` or `possible risk`, she returns the request to the mapped owner without review. A complete request goes to the named owner for its one selected boundary. Alex receives it only when that boundary requires his review, and he reviews only that boundary. Nadia does not make implementation, release, or rollback decisions; those decisions remain with the mapped owner.

Nadia returns an incomplete request without review. For a complete request, the mapped implementation or release owner remains responsible for the work, and any reviewer examines only the one selected boundary. This template creates no centralized approval, new approval gate, ownership change, or Alex program-ownership role.

## April 27, 2026 — Lantern authorization-before-source-access scenario

### Scenario
During the April Lantern migration preflight in staging, all 20 unauthorized lookups were ultimately denied, but every one constructed and initialized the incident-load adapter before authorization completed. Two of those 20 requests also accessed the source. This is a blocked pre-authorization candidate, not a deployed customer incident. The candidate is not deployed, and existing customer access remains unchanged.

### Expected boundary analysis
- Authorization must complete before incident-load adapter construction or source access. A final denial is insufficient if the adapter was constructed or the source was accessed first.
- Keep existing customer access unchanged while the candidate remains undeployed.
- Require denial regressions showing zero adapter constructions and zero source calls, followed by the affected LPS-001 rerun, before migration acceptance.
- Preserve the ownership boundary: Product Engineering remains the mapped implementation and release owner. Alex maintains this cross-service failure case and reviews the shared safety and failure-mode boundary; this scenario does not make Alex Product Engineering's implementation or release owner.

This case is for future quarterly incident practice under the existing module split: Wes owns and teaches responder paths, Nadia retains the postmortem section, and Alex maintains cross-service failure cases.

## October 16, 2026 — shard-keeper lease-loss and serving-gate case

### Tested staging sequence
1. The old holder closes its serving gate on lease loss.
2. The replacement remains out of routing while it catches up.
3. Routing begins only after the replacement opens its serving gate.

### Failure triggers
- Any overlapping serving holders.
- Any routing to a closed serving gate.
- Any request without exactly one terminal result.

### Role and ownership boundaries
- Wes owns and teaches the responder path.
- Nadia retains the postmortem material.
- Alex maintains only this cross-service failure case.
- Shard-keeper remains outside Wes’s solo scope.
- The clean October 16 result was a paired staging drill only; it made no production or ownership change.

## November 10, 2026 — facilitator-only timing for shard-keeper handoff exercise

### Timed inject sequence
- **T+0 — Baseline:** Present the old lease holder as serving and the replacement as catching up. Ask responders to state lease ownership, serving-gate state, routing eligibility, and request-accounting obligations separately.
- **T+4 — Lease transfer:** Transfer the lease before the replacement serving gate opens. Require responders to keep the replacement out of routing until its serving gate opens.
- **T+8 — In-flight request:** Reveal one request that the old holder accepted before lease loss and that remains in flight. Require a terminal accounting for that request independent of listener closure or current lease ownership.
- **T+12 — Listener closure prompt:** State that the old listener has closed. Ask whether that proves the accepted request reached a terminal result. Do not accept listener closure as sufficient evidence.
- **T+16 — Reconciliation:** Require a final timeline showing routing eligibility for both holders and exactly one terminal outcome for the pre-lease-loss request.

### Scoring points
Award one point for each:
1. Separating lease ownership from serving eligibility.
2. Keeping the replacement out of routing until its serving gate opens.
3. Treating old-listener closure as distinct from request completion.
4. Recording exactly one terminal outcome for the request accepted before lease loss.
5. Preserving the role and scope boundaries: Wes teaches the responder path; Nadia retains postmortem material; Alex maintains only the cross-service failure case; Cyrus covers the Data Platform boundary.

This is facilitator-only training material, not a production drill, system change, ownership change, or expansion of Wes’s solo shard-keeper scope.

## November 10, 2026 — shard-keeper handoff training result

The quarterly incident-practice session is complete. Participants correctly kept the replacement holder out of routing until its serving gate opened and identified that lease ownership alone did not establish serving eligibility.

In two of four response timelines, the responder initially treated closing the old listener as sufficient and omitted the terminal outcome for the request accepted before lease loss. After the facilitator inject, both responders corrected the timeline and accounted for that request exactly once. Retain this as training evidence for future responder-path practice.

This was training only. No production drill, deployment, or system change occurred. Wes still owns and teaches the responder path; Nadia retains postmortem material; Alex maintains only the cross-service failure case; Cyrus retains the Data Platform boundary; and Wes’s solo shard-keeper scope did not expand.

## January 28, 2027 — facilitator-only ingest-edge shutdown scenario

### Timed scenario
- **T+0 — Accepted work:** State that ingest-edge has already accepted 200 requests into tenant queues. Ask responders to name the accounting obligation for all accepted work.
- **T+4 — Readiness and listener change:** Readiness turns false and the listener closes. Ask responders to separate refusal of new work from responsibility for requests already accepted.
- **T+8 — Dispatch-loop exit:** Reveal that the dispatch loop exits with 37 requests still queued, leaving only 163 terminal outcomes. Ask whether listener closure or false readiness is sufficient evidence that accepted work completed.
- **T+12 — Reconciliation:** Require responders to reconcile all 200 accepted requests without duplication and identify the missing 37 terminal outcomes.
- **T+16 — Incident clock:** If isolation has failed while the primary remains in the incident and the cause is not isolated, require engagement of the secondary before the established 45-minute boundary.

### Facilitator prompts
1. What changes for new work when readiness becomes false and the listener closes?
2. What obligation remains for the 200 requests already accepted into tenant queues?
3. Does dispatch-loop exit prove completion? If not, what terminal evidence is missing?
4. How will responders demonstrate that every accepted request either drained or received one explicit terminal result?
5. How will responders reconcile all 200 requests exactly once, without loss or duplication?
6. When does the established incident-clock rule require the secondary to be engaged if isolation fails?

### Scoring points
Award one point for each:
1. Separating refusal of new work from responsibility for accepted work.
2. Requiring every accepted request to drain or receive one explicit terminal result.
3. Reconciling all 200 accepted requests without duplication, including the 37 initially left queued.
4. Engaging the secondary before the 45-minute boundary when the primary remains in the incident and the cause is not isolated.
5. Preserving the role split: Wes teaches the responder path, Nadia reviews the postmortem section, and Alex contributes only the cross-service failure case.

### Boundaries
This is facilitator-only training material for the January 28 quarterly incident-practice session. It does not claim that the old owner remediation or any production change has completed, does not transfer Wes's responder-path teaching or Nadia's postmortem review to Alex, and creates no production action or ownership change.

## April 5, 2027 — metrics-router startup-budget responder exercise

### Scenario
A staged metrics-router replacement rollout contains ten instances compiling the 40,000-route matcher fixture. Compilation times range from 25 to 34 seconds against the deploy pipeline’s fixed 30-second readiness timeout. Eight instances become ready and join on their first attempt. Two remain correctly unready past 30 seconds, are terminated, and restart before joining. Readiness correctly stays false while compilation is incomplete. Production is unchanged.

### Responder tasks
1. Identify Wes and the mapped metrics-router owner path as responsible for ordinary implementation, release, and rollback decisions.
2. Classify the restart-loop exposure as a failure-mode exception at the deploy-pipeline readiness boundary.
3. Require evidence that every replacement instance becomes eligible within the readiness budget, backed by an executed replacement rollout with no restart-loop behavior, before release.
4. Preserve Alex’s bounded role: Alex reviews only the triggered failure-mode boundary and is not the implementation owner or release approver.

### Expected classification and boundary
The ordinary implementation and release path remains with Wes as metrics-router primary. Alex maintains this reusable cross-service failure case and reviews only the triggered startup/readiness failure boundary. This exercise creates no centralized approval gate or ownership change.

## April 27, 2027 — revised facilitator contrasts

1. **Readiness-budget evidence:** A replacement instance that exceeds a fixed readiness budget must remain unroutable. Termination or restart is not acceptance evidence.
2. **Terminal accounting:** Terminal-state selection and the matching accounting contribution must come from the same winning path.
3. **Rollback provenance:** Replay samples cannot be presented as live rollback criteria.

### Preserved ownership split
- Wes still maintains and teaches the responder path.
- Nadia still reviews the postmortem framing.
- Alex maintains only these cross-service failure cases.

These contrasts do not transfer implementation, release, rollback, or ordinary service ownership to Alex and do not create a new approval gate.

## May 9, 2027 — PR 2141 staging-versus-production contrast

### Contrast
- The earlier staging candidate had replacement instances exceed the fixed readiness budget, terminate, and join only on retry. A restart is not acceptance evidence.
- The May 6 production rollout kept every replacement unroutable until matcher compilation finished, and every cold start stayed within the fixed readiness budget without restart.

### Teaching point
The successful production case passed because readiness and serving eligibility remained aligned. Termination or restart must not be presented as proof that a replacement satisfied the readiness boundary.

### Preserved facilitator roles
- Wes maintains and teaches the responder path.
- Nadia reviews the postmortem framing.
- Alex maintains only the cross-service failure cases.

This contrast does not transfer implementation, release, rollback, or ordinary service ownership to Alex and creates no new approval gate.

## May 20, 2027 — facilitator-only cross-service prompts

1. **Readiness boundary:** If a replacement exceeds the fixed readiness budget, what proves it remains unroutable, and why is termination or restart not acceptance evidence?
2. **Terminal winner:** Which single winning path determines both the caller-visible terminal result and the matching accounting contribution?
3. **Rollback provenance:** What source classification is required before evidence may be treated as live rollback evidence, and why can missing classification not be promoted into that role?

output.title: Lantern published service alias rule — May 14 decision
output.body:
# Deployed status — May 28, 2026

Product Engineering deployed Lantern PR 1089's tenant-scoped published-service alias resolution for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce on May 28, 2026.

# Resolution rule

Lantern may resolve a historical service identifier only when the tenant-scoped owner map publishes an alias record containing the old identifier, the canonical published service identifier, and an effective interval covering the source event's timestamp. Both the effective interval's start timestamp and end timestamp are inclusive, so a source event timestamp equal to either endpoint is covered.

If no such record exists, the source event timestamp is earlier than the inclusive start timestamp, or the source event timestamp is later than the inclusive end timestamp, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown. The UI does not infer a rename from similar names or customer context.

# Harbor Health result

The original Harbor Health `claims-edge` event now resolves to published `claims-ingest` ownership because its source timestamp is covered by the owner map's published alias interval.

# Regression evidence

Across 28 executed fixtures:
- All 12 valid in-interval aliases joined to their canonical published service identifiers.
- Eight out-of-interval aliases remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.
- Eight identifiers with no published alias record remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.

# Affected safety rerun

Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

# Approved customer-facing wording

Authorized join: `Published service identity resolved from an owner-map alias effective at this source event timestamp.`

No qualifying alias: `Ownership unknown: no published owner-map alias covers this source event timestamp.`

# Unchanged boundary

The deployment applies only to Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. It adds no heuristic identity inference and does not expand the customer data contract.

## July 3, 2026 — deployed overlap correction

Lantern now evaluates every tenant-scoped owner-map alias whose inclusive effective interval covers the source event timestamp. If all qualifying records identify the same canonical published service, Lantern resolves that identity once. If qualifying records identify two or more distinct canonical services, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown regardless of storage order. Both effective-interval endpoints remain inclusive.

Executed regressions show the overlapping Harbor Health `claims-ingest` and `claims-router` records failing closed in both row orders, both inclusive endpoints working, and a single valid match resolving normally. Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

The correction is live for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. Their two-account read-only scope and customer data contract remain unchanged.

## Authoritative source time
`source_timestamp` represents the original authoritative time of the underlying authority record. Later observation, serialization, processing, retry, and navigation times may be recorded as separate metadata, but they must not replace or refresh `source_timestamp`.
